html:
Between 1942 and 1945 the United States government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from the West Coast into camps. About two thirds of them were American citizens.

After the attack on Pearl Harbor, fear and racial prejudice led to demands for their removal. On 19 February 1942 President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, which let the army clear people from military zones. Families had days to sell or leave behind homes and businesses, and were sent to ten camps in remote desert and swamp areas, such as Manzanar and Heart Mountain.

The Supreme Court upheld the policy in Korematsu v. United States in 1944. Many young men still served in the army in segregated units, including the 442nd Regimental Combat Team. In 1988 Congress apologised and paid reparations. It is widely seen as a grave violation of civil rights, during the Pacific War.
